subjective: Nico, a one-year-old male Poodle, has had no dietary changes but has been eating less over the past 3-4 days, now consuming only one to one and a half meals daily. He has a history of gastrointestinal issues, including previous scans and injections for constipation. Owner suspects possible ingestion of a small bone. A tick was found on him two days ago during grooming. Nico has been fussy with appetite and has not eaten since last night. No vomiting reported. He is otherwise active and friendly. Current diet includes boiled chicken (meat removed from bone), boiled pumpkin or carrot, and occasional rice, with chicken liver as a topper to encourage eating. No new supplements except Porgest probiotic. Vaccinations are up to date. Deworming was last done in April. Owner reports occasional diluted stool color but no visible blood. No scooting behavior or anal gland issues noted. Nico is an indoor dog with morning walks.
objective: Physical examination included abdominal palpation and temperature check. Weight measured approximately 8 to 10 kg, slightly decreased from last month (previously 8.15 kg). Stool samples showed diluted color without visible blood. Blood tests have been performed weekly over the past month, showing persistently low platelet counts but no evidence of tick fever. Vaccination records confirm completion of initial and annual vaccines. No fleas or ticks currently observed except one tick found two days ago. No vomiting or other systemic signs observed during examination. Activity level remains normal.
assessment: Nico is exhibiting signs consistent with acute gastroenteritis, possibly hemorrhagic in nature given the diluted stool color and history of gastrointestinal sensitivity common in poodles. Differential diagnoses include dietary indiscretion with possible foreign body ingestion, gastritis, or early infectious causes such as parvovirus, although vaccination status reduces this likelihood. Persistent low platelet counts have been monitored and tick fever has been ruled out. Weight loss and decreased appetite are concerning and warrant further diagnostic evaluation.
plan: Diagnostic: Perform blood tests today to assess for parvovirus and other systemic conditions. Consider abdominal ultrasound if symptoms persist or worsen to rule out foreign body or other abdominal pathology. Therapeutic: Continue probiotics (Porgest) and start Pantoprazole 20 mg, half tablet once daily for 5 days to reduce gastric inflammation. Initiate metronidazole 200 mg, half tablet twice daily with food for intestinal inflammation. Owner to administer medications by wrapping capsules in chicken liver if needed. Preventive: Maintain current vaccination and deworming schedule. Monitoring: Monitor appetite, stool consistency, and activity. Advise owner to report any vomiting, worsening diarrhea, or behavioral changes. Follow-up: Review blood test results and clinical response in 1-2 days. Consider further diagnostics if no improvement.
conclusion: Nico, a one-year-old Poodle with a history of gastrointestinal sensitivity, presents with decreased appetite, diluted stool color without visible blood, and recent weight loss. Physical examination and prior diagnostics including blood tests and abdominal scans have ruled out tick fever and gross abdominal abnormalities. Current clinical signs suggest acute gastroenteritis possibly related to dietary factors or mild gastritis. Treatment with proton pump inhibitor, metronidazole, and probiotics has been initiated. Blood tests are planned to rule out infectious causes such as parvovirus. Owner instructed on medication administration and monitoring. Follow-up is planned to assess response and consider further diagnostics if needed.

1. Acute gastroenteritis with decreased appetite and altered stool consistency; requires monitoring and supportive care.
2. History of gastrointestinal sensitivity and prior constipation requiring intervention.
3. Possible foreign body ingestion considered but previous abdominal scans were normal.
4. Low platelet counts monitored with no evidence of tick fever.
5. Weight loss and fussy eating behavior needing nutritional support and medication.
